newsitem.title: USA: Feds clamp down on groups with Freemen ties - report.
newsitem.headline: Feds clamp down on groups with Freemen ties - report.

text.p: Federal and state authorities have charged or are investigating at least 151 anti-government individuals in 23 states by tracking their links with the Freemen of Montana, the Dallas Morning News reported Saturday.

The newspaper said many of the individuals were among the 800 people who attended $100 seminars at the Freemen ranch on how to produce and issue false money orders, liens and other financial instruments.
The Dallas Morning News said it had identified 65 criminal cases or investigations of conspiracy and fraud involving 151 people with Freemen ties.
Those cases involved false financial instruments that could have totalled $2.17 billion if they had been used successfully, although most were not, the report said.

It was that type of activity that first brought the white supremacist Freemen to the attention of authorities. The Freemen finally surrendered last June at the end of a tense 81-day standoff with the FBI at a remote Montana ranch.

Since then, authorities have used documents found at the ranch as well as federal wiretaps and complaints from businesses and individuals to clamp down on allies or associates of the Freemen in militias and separatist groups across the country.

Freemen leader LeRoy Schweitzer, who taught the seminars, believed the money orders he issued were as legal as those of any bank because the banking system, he said, was illegal and had not been supported by real money since the United States went off the gold standard in 1933.

That belief is shared by many in the anti-government movement. Some of the money orders printed were used to pay federal, state and local taxes while others were used to cover purchases with businesses.
The Freemen refused to pay taxes or have any dealings with the U.S. government which it said was illegitimate.
Declaring their independence from state and federal control, they created their own state on a 960-acre ranch near Jordan on the prairies of eastern Montana, calling it "Justus Township".
